newsitem.title: UK: Spain, Italy bonds celebrate 1996 victory - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Spain, Italy bonds celebrate 1996 victory - Salomon.

text.p: Spanish bonds led the way in 1996, offering investors gains way in excess of core global debt markets in the U.S., Germany and Japan, the Salomon world government bond index showed on Monday.
In peseta terms, holders of Bonos gained a whopping 22.10 percent, pushing Italian bonds into second place with a 21.90-percent return in lira terms.
"EMU-driven yield convergence dominated market performance stories during the year," the Salomon report said.
It said Spanish, Italian and Swedish markets were the top three performers, with investors witnessing 10-year yield spread convergence with Germany of 295, 271 and 161 basis points, respectively.
In dollar terms, Italy held the winning position, gaining 27.19 percent in 1996, while the year's loser was Swiss government debt, which lost investors 9.98 percent.
Japanese bonds offered little more in dollar terms, shedding 6.45 percent. In local currency terms, Japanese bonds managed a positive return of 5.26 percent.
Europe's benchmark, the German Bund market, returned 7.29 percent in marks but lost 0.35 percent in dollars.
Salomon said a strong U.S. dollar versus the yen and mark was one of the major themes in global debt markets in 1996.
The world government bond index as a whole gained 7.43 percent in terms of local currencies but only 3.62 percent in dollars.
"Investors who overweighted high-yielding European markets relative to Germany or overweighted Canada relative to the U.S. would have experienced superior returns," the report said.
Canadian bonds were the best performers outside of Europe, gaining 11.83 percent in local terms and 11.28 percent in U.S. dollars, while Treasuries gained 2.73 percent in dollars.
But Salomon said total returns may have been significantly affected by the relative maturity exposures across the markets.

"Canadian 10-year yields tightened 150 basis points versus the U.S., yet the front end of the curve tightened 250 basis points leading to a bull steepening of the two to 10-year (area) of 112 basis points," it said.
Elsewhere in the dollar bloc, Australian bonds gained 11.75 percent in local terms and 19.32 percent in dollar terms.
Denmark and Britain, both of whom have an opt out clause for European economic and monetary union (EMU), gained 10.49 percent and 7.41 percent, respectively, in local currency terms.
But in dollars, gilts gained a hefty 18.39 percent, while Danish bonds managed only a 3.80 percent.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with over one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
